properties.decision:
`import_graph` writes a node whose `node_ref` property names a node that is in neither the document nor the graph, and names it on `ImportReport.dangling_node_refs` (printed by `--import`). It does NOT fail the import. `create_node` is unchanged and still refuses such a write outright.

ORIGINALLY RECORDED AS PROPOSED, because it was Claude's engineering call taken to keep this design's own export restorable, and it was Anthony's to settle or overturn.

✅ SETTLED 2026-08-29 — ACCEPTED on Anthony's word, after its rationale was corrected twice the same day and a root-cause pass was run on dangling references. He settled the behaviour as drafted: report, do not refuse.
properties.name: A restore reports an unresolvable node reference rather than refusing the whole document
properties.rationale:
THE ALTERNATIVE, and why it lost: refuse the import, matching `create_node`. Measured 2026-08-29 — this design's own export carried nine references written before the guard existed. Under refusal the export could not be restored AT ALL, and the only remedy on offer was hand-editing the export document, which is the one thing this project tells users never to do. Any user upgrading into the guard with a single pre-existing dangling reference would silently acquire an unrestorable backup.

THE DISTINCTION THAT DECIDES IT: a write ASSERTS something new, and refusing a new record about a node the design does not have is right. An import ASSERTS NOTHING — it reproduces a state that already existed, and the document is the evidence that it did. Refusing there is the tool substituting its judgement for a reality it is being handed.

NOT A NEW POLICY. `ImportReport` had already answered this same question three times — `skipped_edges` (an edge whose endpoint is missing is skipped and named, not fatal), `integrity_note` and `provenance_note`, each documented as "the import still proceeds but never silently". A dangling property reference is the other shape of a missing endpoint, so answering it differently would have one import refusing what its neighbour two lines up reports.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
⚠️ CORRECTED TWICE ON 2026-08-29, BEFORE THIS WAS PUT UP FOR A RULING.
The second correction reverses part of the first. Both are kept.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

🛑 ① THE RENAME LEG WAS WITHDRAWN — CORRECTLY, BUT TOO BROADLY. The original said the nine were "five instances of a `prj:`/`proj:` typo, four capabilities renamed after the fact was written" and concluded that "the renames that produce most real dangles are unreachable by ANY write-time check". Measured: those four ids never existed as nodes under any prefix, and the root-cause pass sharpened it further — 6 of the 9 are PREFIX ERRORS on a real slug (`prj:`→`proj:`, `cap:thin-install`→`req:thin-install`) and 3 are slugs INVENTED FROM THE NAME OF A SERVED TOOL. None is a rename. All nine would have been refused at write time.

⭐ ② THE ADMITTED COST IS SMALLER. The original accepted one price — "an export/import laundering route the write guard closes" — as a permanent blind spot. `dangling_reference` (#373) now reports an unresolvable reference on its own terms whatever the node's degree, so anything an import launders in is named on the next sweep rather than never.

🛑🛑 ③ AND THE RETIRE CASE IS REAL AFTER ALL — IT WAS IN THE PROPERTY NOBODY HAD SWEPT. Correction ① was true of `TemporalFact.subject_id` and was over-generalised to the whole class. The root-cause pass swept the other two pointer properties `heal.rs` names, which `fact:defect-seven-temporal-facts-name-a-subject-id-that-does-not-exist` asked for on 2026-08-16 and nobody had done. `Snapshot.target_id` holds 195 values, 191 resolve, and ALL FOUR THAT DANGLE ARE RETIRES — `art:content`, `art:content-test`, `art:tools-content` snapshotted at `epoch:content-store-discontinued`, and `ctr:anthony` at `epoch:the-owners-identity-is-one-node-again`. Every one resolved when written and broke when its target was deleted or merged.

⭐⭐ THIS IS NOW THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT ON THE RECORD FOR REPORTING RATHER THAN REFUSING, and it is measured rather than hypothesised: THOSE FOUR DANGLING REFERENCES ARE CORRECT. A Snapshot exists precisely to preserve what a node was; when the node is deliberately deleted, the snapshot pointing at nothing is the mechanism working, not a fault. So a refusing import would reject this design's own export over four records that are doing their job — and a refusal cannot tell a broken reference from a correct historical one, because at the point of restore they are the same bytes. Only a report can hand that judgement to the person who owns the design.

⚠️ WHAT THAT COSTS THE OTHER SIDE, stated plainly: `Snapshot.target_id` is NOT declared `node_ref`, so those four are invisible to the guard and to `dangling_reference` today, and this argument bites only if anyone declares it. The point stands anyway — the four exist, they are correct, and any rule that treated pointer properties uniformly would refuse them.

📌 WHAT SURVIVES UNTOUCHED, and is what actually carries the decision: assertion versus reproduction, the unrestorable-backup measurement, and the three existing `ImportReport` precedents. None rested on any corrected claim.
